div.head: SUBSECT. 6.
Poverty and want, causes of Melancholy.
div.p: Poverty and want, are so violent oppugners, so unwelcome guests, so much abhorred of all men, that I may not omit to speak of them apart. Poverty, although (if considered aright, to a wise, understanding, truly regenerate, & contented man) it be donum Dei [a gift of God], a blessed estate, the way to Heaven, as Com. ad Hebraeos.Chrysostom calls it, God’s gift, the mother of modesty, & much to be preferred before riches (as shall be showed in his Part. 2 Sect. 3 Memb. 3.place), yet as it is esteemed in the world’s censure, it is a most odious calling, vile and base, a severe torture, summus scelus [the greatest wickedness], a most intolerable burden; we Quem ut difficilem morbum pueris tradere foridamus [Which, like a troublesome illness, we’re afraid of passing on to our children]. Plutarch.shun it all, cane pejus & angue [worse than a dog or a serpent], we abhor the name of it,

lg.l: [Poverty is shunned, and indicted by the whole world,]

div.p: as being the fountain of all other miseries, cares, woes, labours, and grievances whatsoever. To avoid which, we will take any pains, ——— extremos currit mercator ad Indos [the merchant runs to the remotest Indies], we will leave no haven, no coast, no creek of the world unsearched, though it be to the hazard of our lives, we will dive to the bottom of the sea, to the bowels of the earth, As in the silver mines at Freiburg in Germany. Fynes Moryson.five, six, seven, eight, nine hundred fathom deep, through all five Zones, and both extremes of heat and cold: we will turn parasites and slaves, prostitute ourselves, swear and lie, damn our bodies and souls, forsake God, abjure Religion, steal, rob, murder, rather than endure this unsufferable yoke of Poverty, which doth so tyrannize, crucify, and generally depress us.

For look into the world, and you shall see men most part esteemed according to their means, and happy as they are rich: Euripides.Ubique tanti quisque quantum habuit fuit [each man everywhere is worth as much as he owns]. If he be likely to thrive, & in the way of preferment, who but he? In the vulgar opinion, if a man be wealthy, no matter how he gets it, of what parentage, how qualified, how virtuously endowed, or villainously inclined; let him be a bawd, a gripe, an usurer, a villain, a Pagan, a Barbarian, a wretch, Tom. 4. dial.Lucian’s tyrant, on whom you may look with less security, than on the Sun: so that he be rich (and liberal withal) he shall be honoured, admired, adored, reverenced, and highly Omnis enim res, virtus, fama, decus, divina, humanaque pulchris Divitiis parent [For everything – virtue, fame, honour, things divine and human – is subject to the beauty of wealth]. Hor. Ser. lib. 2 Sat. 3. Clarus erit fortis, justus, sapiens etiam rex. Et quicquid volet [{The rich man} will be famous, brave, just, wise, even a king, and whatsoever he wants]. Hor.magnified. The rich is
had in reputation because of his goods, Eccl. 10. 31. He shall be befriended: for, riches gather many friends, Prov. 19. 4; ——— multos numerabit amicos [he’ll count many friends], all Et genus, & formam, regina pecunia donat [Queen Money grants both birth and beauty]. Money adds spirits, courage, &c.happiness ebbs and flows with his money. He shall be accounted a gracious Lord, a Maecenas, a benefactor, a wise, discreet, a proper, a valiant, a fortunate man, of a generous spirit, Pullus Jovis, & gallinae filius albae [Jove’s chick and the son of a white hen]: a hopeful, a good man, a virtuous, honest man. Quando ego te Junonium puerum, & matris partum vere aurem [When I {called} you ‘Juno’s boy’, and your mother’s birth-giving ‘golden’], as Epist. ult. ad Atticum.Tully said of Octavianus, while he was adopted Caesar, & an Our young Master, a fine towardly gentleman, God bless him, & hopeful; why? He is heir apparent to the right worshipful, to the right honourable, &c.heir apparent of so great a Monarchy, he was a golden child. All O nummi, nummi: vobis hunc praestat honorem [O money, money! He pays this honour to you].honour, offices, applause, grand titles, and turgent Epithets are put upon him, omnes omnia bona dicere [everyone says all good things]; all men’s eyes are upon him, God bless his good worship, his honour; Exinde sapere eum omnes dicimus, ac quisque fortunam habet [We all judge a man’s wisdom by the size of his fortune]. Plaut. Pseud.every man speaks well of him, every man presents him, seeks and sues to him for his love, favour & protection, to serve him, belong unto him, every man riseth to him, as to Themistocles in the Olympics, if he speak, as of Herod, Vox Dei, non hominis, the voice of God, not of man. All the graces, Veneres, pleasures, elegances attend him, Julius Capitolinus vita Antonini.golden Fortune accompanies and lodgeth with him; and as to those Roman Emperors, is placed in his chamber.

lg.l: ——— Petronius.Secura naviget aura,
[… He sails in a fair wind,
And governs Fortune with his will:]

div.p:
he may sail as he will himself, and temper his estate at his pleasure, Jovial days, splendour and magnificence, sweet Music, dainty fare, the good things, and fat of the land, fine clothes, rich attires, soft beds, down pillows are at his command, all the world labours for him, thousands of Artificers are his slaves to drudge for him, run, ride, and post for him: Theologi opulentis adhaerent, Jurisperiti pecuniosis, literati nummosis, liberalibus artifices, &c. [Theologians cling to the wealthy, legal practitioners to the moneyed, scholars to the rich, artists to the bountiful, etc.]Divines (for Pythia Philippisat [Pythia philippized]), Lawyers, Physicians, Philosophers, Scholars are his, wholly devote to his service. Every man seeks his Multi illum juvenes, multae petiere puellae [Many young men, many girls have sought that man out].acquaintance, his kindred, to match with him, though he be an aufe, a ninny, a monster, a goose-cap,
uxorem ducat Danaen [let him take Danae as his wife], when, and whom he will, hunc optant generum Rex & Regina [the king and queen choose him for a son-in-law] –—— he is an excellent Dummodo sit dives barbarus, ille placet [Even if the wealthy man is a barbarian, he’ll do].match for my son, my daughter, my niece, &c. Quicquid calcaverit hic, Rosa fiet [Whatever he treads on will become a rose], let him go whither he will, Trumpets sound, Bells ring, &c., all happiness attends him, every man is willing to entertain him, he sups in Plut. in Lucullo, a rich Chamber so called.Apollo wheresoever he comes; what preparation is made for his Panis pane melior [Bread better than bread].entertainment? Fish & fowl, spices and perfumes, all that sea and land affords. What cookery, masquing, mirth to exhilarate his person?

l.hi: Da Trebio, pone ad Trebium, vis frater ab illis

lg.l: Ilibus? ———
[Give Trebius some, serve it to Trebius! Brother, would you like some of that Loin? …]

div.p: What dish will your good worship eat of?

lg.l: ——— Hor. Sat. 5 lib. 2.dulcia poma,

l.hi: Et quoscunque feret cultus tibi fundus honores,

lg.l: Ante Larem, gustet venerabilior Lare dives.
Sweet apples, and what e’er thy fields afford,
Before thy Gods be serv’d, let serve thy Lord.

div.p:
What sport will your honour have? Hawking, hunting, fishing, fowling, bulls, bears, cards, dice, cocks, players, tumblers, fiddlers, jesters, &c., they are at your good worship’s command. Fair houses, gardens, orchards, terraces, galleries, cabinets, pleasant walks, delightsome places, they are at hand; Bohemus de Turcis, & Breydenbach.in aureis lac, vinum in argenteis, adolescentulae ad nutum speciosae [milk in gold cups, wine in silver ones, beautiful young girls at his command], wine, wenches, &c., a Turkey Paradise, heaven upon earth. Though he be a silly soft fellow, and scarce have common sense, yet if he be born to fortunes (as I have said) Euphormio.jure haereditario sapere jubetur, he must be wise, Qui pecuniam habent, elati sunt animi [Whoever has money, has exalted spirits]: lofty spirits, brave men-at-arms, all rich men are generous, courageous, &c.valiant and discreet by inheritance, he must have honour and office in his course: Nemo nisi dives honore dignus [no one deserves honour except the rich man] (Ambros. 2 offic. 21), none so worthy as himself: he shall have it, atque esto quicquid Servius aut Labeo [and be all that Servius and Labeo were]. Get money enough, & command Nummus ait Pro me nubat Cornubia Romae [Money says, ‘It was for my sake that Cornwall wedded Rome’].Kingdoms, Provinces, Armies, Hearts, Hands, and Affections; thou shalt have
Popes, Patriarchs to be thy Chaplains and Parasites; thou shalt have (Tamerlane-like) Kings to draw thy Coach, Queens to be thy Laundresses, Emperors thy footstools, build more Towns and Cities than great Alexander, Babel Towers, Pyramids & Mausolean Tombs, &c., command heaven and earth, and tell the world it is thy vassal, auro emitur diadema, argento coelum panditur, denarius Philosophum conducit, nummus jus cogit, obolus literatum pascit, metallum sanitatem conciliat, aes amicos conglutinat [a diadem is bought with gold, heaven is opened up with silver, a penny hires a philosopher, a shilling controls justice, a halfpenny feeds the man of letters, cash provides health, money binds friends together]. And therefore not without good cause, Flor. hist.John Medices that rich Florentine, when he lay upon his deathbed, calling his sons, Cosmus & Laurence before him, amongst other sober sayings, repeated this, Animo quieto digredior, quod vos sanos & divites post me relinquam, it doth me good to think yet, though I be dying, that I shall leave you my children, Sound and Rich: for wealth sways all. It is not with us, as amongst those Lacedaemonian Senators of Lycurgus in Plutarch, He preferred that deserved best, was most virtuous and worthy of the place, not swiftness, or strength, or wealth, or friends carried it in those days; but inter optimos optimus, inter temperantes temperantissimus [among the excellent, the best, among the sober, the soberest], the most temperate & best. We have no Aristocracies but in contemplation, all Oligarchies, wherein a few rich men domineer, do what they list and are privileged by their greatness. Quicquid libet licet [Whatever you like, it’s permitted].They may freely trespass, and do as they please, no man dare accuse them, no not so much as mutter against them, there is no notice taken of it, they may securely do it, live after their own laws, and for their money get pardons, indulgences, redeem their souls from Purgatory and Hell itself, ——— clausum possidet arca Jovem [Jupiter’s shut up inside the money box]. Let them be Epicures, or Atheists, Libertines, Machiavellians (as often they are),

l.hi: Et quamvis perjurus erit, sine gente, cruentus,

lg.l: [And however perjured he may be, low-born, bloodstained,]

div.p:
they may go to heaven through the eye of a needle, if they will themselves, they may be canonized for Saints, they shall be Cum moritur dives concurrunt undique cives: Pauperis ad funus vix est ex millibus unus [When a rich man dies, citizens from all places rush over together; at the funeral of a pauper there’s barely one out of all the thousands].honourably interred in Mausolean tombs, commended by Poets, registered in histories, have temples and statues erected to their names, ——— e manibus illis ——— nascentur violae ——— [from those remains … violets will grow]. If he be bountiful in his life, & liberal at his death, he shall have one to swear, as he did by Claudius the Emperor in Tacitus, he saw his soul go to Heaven, and be miserably lamented at his funeral, ambubaiarum collegia, &c. [guilds of flute-girls, etc.] Trimalchionis Topanta in Petronius recta in coelum abiit, went right to Heaven: a base quean, thou wouldst have scorned once in thy misery to have a penny from her; and
why? Modio nummos metiis, she measured her money by the bushel. These prerogatives do not usually belong to rich men, but to such as are most part seeming rich, let him have but a good He that wears silk, satin, velvet, and gold lace, must needs be a gentleman.outside, he carries it, and shall be adored for a God, as Xenophon Cyropaed. lib. 8.Cyrus was amongst the Persians, ob splendidum apparatum, for his gay tires; now most men are esteemed according to their clothes. In our gullish times, him whom you peradventure in modesty would give place to, as being deceived by his habit, and presuming him some great worshipful man, believe it, if you shall examine his estate, he will likely be proved a serving-man of no great note, my Lady’s Tailor, his Lordship’s Barber, or some such gull, a Fastidious Brisk, Sir Petronel Flash, a mere outside. Only this respect is given him, that wheresoever he comes, he may call for what he will, and take place by reason of his outward habit.

But on the contrary, if he be poor, Prov. 15. 15, all his days are miserable, he is under hatches, dejected, rejected and forsaken, poor in purse, poor in spirit; Euripides.prout res nobis fluit, ita & animus se habet, Est sanguis atque spiritus pecunia mortalibus [Money is the blood and spirit of mortals].money gives life & soul. Though he be honest, wise, learned, well-deserving, noble by birth, and of excellent good parts: yet in that he is poor, unlikely to rise, come to honour, office or good means, he is contemned, neglected, frustra sapit, inter literas esurit, amicus molestus [he’s wise in vain, he’s hungry amid his books, he’s an irksome friend]. In tenui rara est facundia panno [Eloquence rarely appears in shabby clothing]. Juven.If he speak, what babbler is this? Ecclus. His nobility without wealth, is Hor.projecta vilior alga [worth less than beached seaweed], and he not esteemed: Nos viles pulli nati infelicibus ovis [we’re common chicks hatched from cursed eggs], if once poor, we are metamorphosed in an instant, base slaves, villains and vile drudges; Egere est offendere & indigere scelestum esse [To be destitute is to offend, and to be needy is wicked]. Sat. menip.for to be poor, is to be a knave, a fool, a wretch, a wicked, an odious fellow, a common eyesore, say poor and say all: they are born to labour, to misery, to carry burdens like juments, pistum stercus comedere [to eat mashed dung] with Ulysses’ companions, and as Chremylus objected in Aristophanes, Plutus act. 4.salem lingere, lick salt, to empty jakes, fay channels, Nullum tam barbarum, tam vile munus est, quod non lubentissime obire velit gens vilissima [No service is so barbarous, so vile, that this most vile people won’t most readily want to perform it].carry out dirt and dunghills, sweep chimneys, rub horse heels, &c. I say nothing of Turks’ Galley-slaves, which are bought Lansius orat. in Hispaniam.and sold like juments, or those African Negroes, or poor Laet. descript. Americae.Indian drudges, qui indies hinc inde deferendis oneribus occumbunt, nam quod apud nos boves & asini vehunt, trahunt, &c., id omne misellis Indis, &c. [who daily fall dying under the burdens they’re bearing from here to there, for what oxen and asses carry and drag for us, etc., all that’s done
by the poor Indians, etc.], they are ugly to behold, and though erst spruce, now rusty and squalid, because poor, Plautus.immundus fortunas aequum est squalorem sequi [it’s fitting for filthy luck to result in squalor], it is ordinarily so. Leo Afer cap. ult. lib. 1. Heinsius.Others eat to live, but they live to drudge, Munster de rusticis Germaniae Cosmog. cap. 27 lib. 3.servilis & misera gens nihil recusare audet, a servile generation, that dare refuse no task.

lg.l: ——— Ter. Eunuch.Heus tu Dromo,

foreign.hi: Cape hoc flabellum, ventulum hinc facito dum lavamus,

div.p:
Sirrah blow wind upon us while we wash, and bid your fellow get him up betimes in the morning, be it fair or foul, he shall run 50 miles afoot tomorrow, to carry me a Letter to my mistress, Socia ad pistrinam, Socia shall tarry at home and grind malt all day long, Tristan thresh. Thus are they commanded, being indeed some of them as so many footstools for rich men to tread on, blocks for them to get on horseback, or as Pauper paries factus, quem caniculae commingant [The pauper is made a wall for small dogs to piss on].walls for them to piss on. They are commonly such people, rude, silly, superstitious Idiots, nasty, unclean, lousy, poor, dejected, slavishly humble: and as Lib. 1 cap. ult.Leo Afer observes of the commonalty of Africk, natura viliores sunt, nec apud suos duces majore in precio quam si canes essent: Deos omnes illis infensos diceres: tam pannosi, fame fracti tot assidue malis afficiuntur, tanquam pecora quibus splendor rationis emortuus [You would have said that all the gods were inimical to them, they’re so tattered and shattered by hunger, and continually afflicted with so many evils, as if they’re beasts in whom the brightness of reason has been extinguished].base by nature, and no more esteemed than dogs, miseram, laboriosam, calamitosam vitam agunt, & inopem, infaelicem, rudiores asinis, ut e brutis plane natos dicas [they live such a wretched, toilsome, calamitous life, so destitute, unhappy, wilder than asses, that you’d simply say they were the offspring of brutes]: no learning, no knowledge, no civility, scarce common sense, naught but barbarism amongst them, belluino more vivunt, neque calceos gestant, neque vestes, like rogues and vagabonds, they go barefooted and bare-legged, the soles of their feet being as hard as horse-hoofs, as Peregrin. Hieros.Radzivilius observed at Damiata in Egypt, leading a laborious, miserable, wretched, unhappy life, Leo Afer.like beasts and juments, if not worse (for a Bartholomaeus à Casa.Spaniard in Yucatan, sold three Indian boys for a Cheese, and an hundred Negro slaves for an horse): their discourse is scurrility, their summum bonum [highest good], a pot of Ale. There is not any slavery which these villains will not undergo, inter illos plerique latrinas evacuant, alii culinariam curant, alii stabularios agunt, urinatores, & id genus similia exercent, &c. [among them many empty latrines, others look after the kitchen, others act as stable-boys, as divers, and work in
similar kinds of job], like those people that dwell in the Ortelius in Helvetia. Qui habitant in Caesia valle ut plurimum latomi, in Oscella valle cultrorum fabri, fumarii in Vegetia, sordidum genus hominum, quod repurgandis caminis victum parat [Those who inhabit the valley of Caesia are mostly stone-cutters, in the valley of Oscella makers of ploughshares, in Vegetia sweeps, a sordid race of men who get their sustenance from cleaning chimneys].Alps, Chimney-sweepers, Jakes farmers, Dirt-daubers, Vagrant rogues, they labour hard some, and yet cannot get clothes to put on, or bread to eat. For what can filthy poverty give else, but I write not this anyways to upbraid, or scoff at, or misuse poor men, but rather to condole and pity them, by expressing, &c.beggary, fulsome nastiness, squalor, contempt, drudgery, labour, ugliness, hunger and thirst: pediculorum, & pulicum numerum, as Chremylus Act. 4 Plut.he well followed it in Aristophanes, fleas and lice, pro pallio vestem laceram, & pro pulvinari lapidem bene magnum ad caput, rags for his raiment, and a stone for his pillow, pro cathedra, ruptae caput urnae, he sits in a broke pitcher, or on a block for a chair, & malvae ramos pro panibus comedit, he drinks water, and lives on wort leaves, pulse, like a hog, or scraps like a dog, ut nunc nobis vita afficitur, quis non putabit insaniam esse, infelicitatemque? as Chremylus concludes his speech, as we poor men live nowadays, who will not take our life to be Paupertas durum onus miseris mortalibus [Poverty is a harsh burden on miserable mortals].infelicity, misery and madness?

If they be of little better condition than those base villains, hunger-starved beggars, wandering rogues, those ordinary slaves, and day-labouring drudges; yet they are commonly so preyed upon by Vexat censura columbas [The censorship persecutes the doves].polling officers for breaking laws, by their tyrannizing Landlords, so flayed and fleeced by perpetual Deux ace non possunt, & six cinque solvere nolunt: omnibus est notum quater tre solvere totum [Two and one can’t pay, and six and five won’t; everyone knows that four and three pay the lot].exactions, that though they do drudge, fare hard, and starve their Genius, they cannot live in some Scandia, Africa, Lithuania, Turcia, &c.countries; but what they have is instantly taken from them, the very care they take to live, to be drudges, to maintain their poor families, their trouble and anxiety takes away their sleep, Sirac. 31. 1, it makes them weary of their lives: when they have taken all pains, done their utmost and honest endeavours, if they be cast behind by sickness, or overtaken with years, no man pities them, hard-hearted and merciless, uncharitable as they are, they leave them so distressed, to beg, steal, murmur and Montaigne in his Essays speaks of certain Indians in France, that being asked how they liked the country, wondered how a few rich men could keep so many poor men in subjection, that they did not cut their throats.rebel, or else starve. The feeling and fear of this misery compelled those old Romans, whom Menenius Agrippa pacified, to resist their governors: outlaws, and rebels in most places, to take up seditious arms, and in all ages hath caused uproars, murmurings, seditions, rebellions, thefts, murders, mutinies, jars and contentions in every commonwealth: grudging, repining, complaining, discontent in each private family, because they want
means to live according to their callings, bring up their children, it breaks their hearts, they cannot do as they would. No greater misery than for a Lord to have a Knight’s living, a Gentleman a Yeoman’s, not to be able to live as his birth and place requires. Poverty and want are generally corrosives to all kind of men, especially to such as have been in good and flourishing estate, are suddenly distressed, Augustas animas animoso in pectore versant [They vex their venerable souls within their bold breasts].nobly born, liberally brought up, and by some disaster and casualty, miserably dejected. For the rest, as they have base fortunes, so have they base minds correspondent, like Beetles e stercore orti, e stercore victus, in stercore delicium [born from dung, nourished on dung, relishing dung], as they were obscurely born and bred, so they delight and live in obscenity; they are not so thoroughly touched with it.

lg.l: Angustas animas angusto in pectore versant.
[Straitened souls dwell in straitened breasts.]

div.p: Yea, that which is no small cause of their torments, if once they come to be in distress, they are forsaken of their fellows, most part neglected, and left unto themselves; as poor Donatus vit. ejus.Terence in Rome was by Scipio, Laelius, and Furius, his great and noble friends.

l.hi: Nil Publius Scipio profuit, nil ei Laelius, nil Furius,
Tres per idem tempus qui agitabant nobiles facillime,

lg.l: Horum ille opera ne domum quidem habuit conductitiam.
[Publius Scipio wasn’t any use to him, neither was Laelius, nor Furius,
The three noblemen at that time who lived most comfortably,
He didn’t even get a rented house with their help.]

div.p: ’Tis generally so, Tempora si fuerint nubila, solus eris [if the weather turns cloudy, you’ll be alone], he is left cold and comfortless, nullus ad amissas ibit amicus opes [no friend will come when wealth is lost], all flee from him as from a rotten wall, now ready to fall on their heads. Prov. 19. 4, Poverty separates them from their Prov. 19. 7, though he be instant yet they will not.neighbours.

l.hi: Dum fortuna favet, vultum servatis amici,

lg.l: Cum cecidit, turpi vertitis ora fuga.
Whilst fortune favour’d, friends, you smil’d on me.
But when she fled, a friend I could not see.

div.p: Which is worse yet, if he be poor Non est qui doleat vicem, ut Petrus Christum jurant se hominem non novisse [No man would suffer in another’s place: they swear they don’t know the man, like Peter did Christ].every man contemns him, insults over him, oppresseth him, scoffs at, aggravates his misery.

l.hi: Quum coepit quassata domus subsidere, partes

lg.l: In proclinatas omne recumbit onus.
When once the tottering house begins to shrink,
Thither comes all the weight by an instinct.

div.p: Nay they are odious to their own brethren, and dearest friends, Prov. 19. 7. His brethren hate him if he be poor, Horat.omnes vicini oderunt, his neighbours hate him, Prov. 14. 20. Ter. Eunuchus act. 2 sc. 2.Omnes me noti ac ignoti deserunt, as he complained in the Comedy, friends & strangers, all forsake me. Which is most grievous, poverty makes men ridiculous, Nil habet infelix paupertas durius in se, quam quod ridiculos homines facit, they must endure Quid quod materiam praebet causamque jocandi. Si toga sordida sit [And what of the fact that he supplies matter and cause for joking? If his cloak is dirty]. Juv. Sat. 3.jests, taunts, flouts, blows of their betters, and take all in good part to get a meal’s meat: Hor.magnum pauperies oppobrium, jubet quidvis & facere & pati [poverty’s a great disgrace, it commands us to do and suffer anything]. He must turn Parasite, jester, fool, cum desipientibus desipere [to be foolish with the fools], saith In Phoeniss.Euripides, slave, villain, drudge to get a poor living, applying himself to each man’s humours, to win & please, &c., and be buffeted, when he hath all done, as Ulysses was by Melanthius Odyss. 17.in Homer, be reviled, baffled, insulted over, for Idem.potentiorum stultitia perferenda est [the stupidity of the powerful must be endured], and may not so much as mutter against it. He must turn rogue, and villain; for as the saying is, Necessitas cogit ad turpia [necessity compels to shameful actions], poverty alone makes men thieves, rebels, murderers, traitors, assassinates, because of poverty we have sinned, Ecclus. 27. 1, swear & forswear, bear false witness, lie, dissemble, anything, as I say, to advantage themselves, and to relieve their necessities: Mantuan.Culpae scelerisque magistra est [it’s the teacher of guilt and crime], when a man is driven to his shifts, what will he not do?

lg.l: ——— si miserum fortuna Sinonem

l.hi: Finxit, vanum etiam mendacemque improba finget,

lg.l: [… If Fortune has made Sinon an object of pity,
Shamelessly, she’ll also make him a liar and a cheat,]

div.p:
he will betray his father, Prince, and country, turn Turk, forsake Religion, abjure God and all, nulla tam horrenda proditio, quam illi lucri causa (saith De Africa lib. 1 cap. ult.Leo Afer) perpetrare nolint [there’s no treachery so horrible, that for profit’s sake … they’re unwilling to commit it]. 4 de legibus.Plato therefore calls poverty, thievish, sacrilegious, filthy, wicked and mischievous; and well he might. For it makes many an upright
man otherwise, had he not been in want, to take bribes, to be corrupt, to do against his conscience, to sell his tongue, heart, hand, &c., to be churlish, hard, unmerciful, uncivil, to use indirect means to help his present estate. It makes Princes to exact upon their subjects, Great men tyrannize, Landlords oppress, Justice mercenary, Lawyers vultures, Physicians Harpies, friends importunate, tradesmen liars, honest men thieves, devout assassinates, great men to prostitute their wives, daughters & themselves, middle sort to repine, commons to mutiny, all to grudge, murmur and complain. A great temptation to all mischief, it compels some miserable wretches to counterfeit several diseases, to dismember, make themselves blind, lame, to have a more plausible cause to beg, and lose their limbs to recover their present wants. Jodocus Damhoderius a Lawyer of Bruges, praxi rerum criminal. cap. 112, hath some notable examples of such counterfeit Cranks, and every village almost will yield abundant testimonies amongst us; we have Dummerers, Abraham men; &c. And that which is the extent of misery, it enforceth them through anguish and wearisomeness of their lives, to make away themselves: they had rather be hanged, drowned, &c., than to live without means.

l.hi: In mare caetiferum, ne te premat aspera egestas,

lg.l: Desili, & a celsis corrue Cerne jugis.
Much better ’tis to break thy neck,
Or drown thy self i’th’ Sea,
Than Suffer irksome poverty,
Go make thyself away.

div.p:
A Sybarite of old, as I find it registered in Dipnosophist. lib. 12.Athenaeus, supping in Phiditiis in Sparta, and observing their hard fare, said it was no marvel if the Lacedaemonians were valiant men; for his part he would rather run upon a sword point (and so would any man in his wits) than live with such base diet, or lead so wretched a life. Gasper Vilela Jesuita epist. Japon. lib.In Japonia ’tis a common thing to stifle their children if they be poor, or to make an abort, which Aristotle commends. In that civil commonwealth of China, Mat. Riccius expedit. in Sinas lib. 1 cap. 3.the mother strangles her child, if she be not able to bring it up, and had rather lose, than sell it, or have it endure such misery as poor men do. Arnobius lib. 7 adversus gentes, Lactantius lib. 5 cap. 9, object as much to those ancient Greeks and Romans, they did expose their children to wild beasts, strangle, or knock out their brains against a stone, in such cases. If we may give credit to Cosmog. 4 lib. cap. 22.Munster, amongst us Christians in Lithuania, they voluntarily mancipate, and sell themselves, their wives and children to rich men, to avoid hunger and beggary; Vel bonorum desperatione, vel malorum perpessione fracti & fatigati, plures violentas manus sibi inferunt [Shattered and exhausted either by the despair of comforts or by the suffering of evils, many lay violent hands on themselves].many make away themselves in this extremity. Apicius the Roman, when he cast up his accounts, and found but
100,000 Crowns left, murdered himself for fear he should be famished to death. P. Forestus in his medicinal observations, hath a memorable example, of two brothers of Louvain, that being destitute of means, became both melancholy, & in a discontented humour massacred themselves. Another of a merchant, learned, wise otherwise and discreet, but out of a deep apprehension he had of a loss at Seas, would not be persuaded but as Hor.Ventidius in the Poet, he should die a beggar. In a word thus much I may conclude of poor men, that though they have good Ingenio poteram superas volitare per arces, Ut me pluma levat, sic grave mergit onus [By my genius I could have flown through the citadels of heaven. As my feathers lift me, so my heavy burden sinks me]. Alciat.parts, they cannot show or make use of them: Paschalius.ab inopia ad virtutem obsepta est via, ’tis hard for a poor man to rise, haud facile emergunt, quorum virtutibus obstat res angusta domi [they don’t easily ascend whose virtues are hindered by straitened means]: the wisdom of the poor is despised, and his words are not heard. Eccles. 9. 16. His works are rejected, contemned, for the baseness and obscurity of the author, though laudable and good in themselves, they will not likely take.

l.hi: Nulla placere diu, neque vivere carmina possunt,

lg.l: Quae scribuntur aquae potoribus. ———
[No poems can please for long, or survive,
Which are written by water-drinkers …]

div.p: Poor men cannot please, their actions, counsels, consultations, projects, are vilified in the world’s esteem, Terent.amittunt consilium in re [they lose their sense with their possessions], which Gnatho long since observed. Hor. Sat. 3 lib. 1.Sapiens crepidas sibi nunquam nec soleas fecit, a wise man never cobbled shoes; as he said of old, but how doth he prove it? I am sure we find it otherwise in our days, Petronius.pruinosis horret facundia pannis [eloquence shivers in frosty rags]. Homer himself must beg if he wants means, and as by report sometimes he did, Herodotus vita ejus. Scaliger in Poet.go from door to door, and sing ballads, with a company of boys about him. This common misery of theirs must needs distract, make them discontent and melancholy, as ordinarily they are, wayward, peevish, like a weary travailer, for

l.hi: Fames & mora bilem in nares conciunt,

lg.l: [Hunger and delay get up your nose,]

div.p: still murmuring and repining: Ob inopiam morosi sunt, quibus est male [because of their helplessness, the sick are hard to please], as Plutarch quotes out of Euripides, and that comical Poet well seconds,

foreign.hi: Omnes quibus res sunt minus secundae, nescio quomodo
Suspitiosi, ad contumeliam omnia accipiunt magis,

lg.l: Propter suam impotentiam se credunt negligi.

div.p: If they be in adversity, they are more suspicious and apt to mistake; they think themselves scorned by reason of their misery; and therefore many generous spirits in such cases, withdraw themselves from all company, as that Comedian Donat. vita. ejus.Terence is said to have done; when he perceived himself to be forsaken and poor, he voluntarily banished himself, to Stymphalus a base town in Arcadia, and there miserably died.

lg.l: ——— ad summam inopiam redactus,
Itaque e conspectu omnium abiit Graeciae in terram ultimam.
[… Reduced to extreme poverty,
So he vanished from everyone’s sight to the remotest part of Greece.]

div.p: Neither is it without cause, for we see men commonly respected according to their means (Euripides.an dives sit, omnes quaerunt, nemo an bonus [everyone asks whether he’s rich, nobody whether he’s good]), and vilified if they be in bad clothes. Plutarch vita ejus.Philopoemen the Orator was set to cut wood, because he was so homely attired, Vita. Ter.Terentius was placed at lower end of Caecilius’ table, because of his homely outside. Gomesius lib. 3 cap. 21 de sale.Dante that famous Italian Poet by reason his clothes were but mean, could not be admitted to sit down at a feast. Gnatho scorned his old familiar friend because of his apparel, Ter. Eunuch. Act. 2 Scen. 2.Hominem video pannis, annisque obsitum, hic ego illum contempsi prae me [I saw a man overgrown with rags and years; at this, comparing him with myself, I felt contempt for him]. King Perseus overcome sent a letter to Liv. dec. 9 lib. 2.Paulus Aemilius the Roman General; Perseus P. Consuli. S. [Perseus to Paullus the consul, greetings], but he scorned him any answer, tacite exprobans fortunam suam (saith mine author), upbraiding him with his present fortune. Cominaeus.Carolus Pugnax, that great Duke of Burgundy, made H. Holland, late Duke of Exeter, exiled, run after his horse like a lackey, and would take no notice of him: He that hath 5 l. per annum coming in more than others, scorns him that hath less, and is a better man.’tis the common fashion of the world. So that such men as are poor may justly be discontent, melancholy, and complain of their present misery, and all may pray with Prov. 30. 8.Solomon, Give me O lord neither riches nor poverty, feed me with food convenient for me.
